question: Which muscle acts as a gatekeeper, controlling the passage of food from the stomach into the small intestine?
explanation: You've got this! The pyloric sphincter sits at the lower end of the stomach, acting like a tap to control when digested food moves into the small intestine.

question: In which part of the abdomen is the main portion of the stomach located?
explanation: Think of the abdomen in four quarters. The stomach rests comfortably right up in the upper left section, just below your diaphragm.

question: What are the temporary folds inside the stomach that flatten out when you eat a big meal called?
explanation: Rugae are like little accordion folds in the stomach lining. They let the stomach stretch safely when you enjoy a heavy meal!

question: Why does the stomach have an extra layer of muscle compared to other parts of the digestive tract?

options.A: To allow vigorous multi-directional churning of solid food
options.B: To absorb nutrients directly into the bloodstream very quickly
options.C: To store extra blood supply for active digestive processes
options.D: To prevent digestive enzymes from burning through the wall

explanation: Food isn't always liquid! That extra muscle layer gives the stomach extra power to twist and mash solid food into a smooth mixture.

question: Which special cells in the stomach lining make hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor?
explanation: Parietal cells are the acid-makers of the stomach, and they also produce intrinsic factor which helps your body absorb vitamin B12.

question: What is the main job of pepsinogen, which is released by the chief cells?

options.A: It neutralizes stomach acid to protect the delicate intestinal lining
options.B: It stimulates the pancreas to release digestive enzymes
options.C: It breaks down proteins after being converted to active pepsin
options.D: It lubricates food particles so they slide easily down the esophagus

explanation: Chief cells release pepsinogen in a safe, inactive form. Once stomach acid turns it into pepsin, it gets straight to work digesting proteins from your food.

question: What do we call the action where food is pushed back inside the stomach to get mashed up even more?
explanation: Think of retropulsion as the stomach's bounce-back action. Food gets pushed toward the closed exit valve and bounces back for another round of mixing!

question: How does the stomach manage to hold a large meal without building up uncomfortable pressure inside?

options.A: By instantly secreting massive amounts of extra mucus
options.B: Through receptive relaxation of its muscular wall
options.C: By opening the pyloric sphincter immediately
options.D: Through rapid absorption of water into the stomach wall

explanation: Your stomach is brilliantly designed! As food enters, the muscles proactively relax to accommodate the meal so you don't feel uncomfortably bloated right away.

question: Which stage of digestion gets triggered simply by the sight, smell, or even thought of delicious food?
explanation: Ever start salivating just thinking about jollof rice? That's the cephalic phase at work—your brain priming your digestive system before food even touches your lips!

question: When a patient eats a heavy protein meal, which hormone is released to trigger heavy acid and enzyme production?
explanation: Gastrin is the signal booster! When protein arrives and stretches the stomach, gastrin is released to tell the stomach to produce more acid for digestion.

question: Which of the following is NOT a main cause of peptic ulcers?
explanation: While spicy or salty foods can irritate an existing ulcer, they don't cause them on their own. Ulcers are mainly caused by H. pylori bacteria and regular use of NSAID painkillers.

question: Why do common pain relievers like ibuprofen (NSAIDs) often lead to stomach irritation and ulcers?

options.A: They inhibit prostaglandins that build the protective stomach mucus layer
options.B: They stimulate the vagus nerve to release toxic amounts of pepsinogen
options.C: They paralyze the pyloric sphincter causing food to back up dangerously
options.D: They directly transform into hydrochloric acid inside the gastric lumen

explanation: NSAIDs block helpful chemicals called prostaglandins. Without them, the stomach loses some of its natural protective mucus lining and gets exposed to acid.
